t: How To Test Your Class Rules
q: It’s to form an impenetrable boundary that keeps misbehavior out and the freedom to teach in.
Outside of the square, write down every misbehavior you can think of that you’ve witnessed in the past five years—or for as long as you’ve been teaching.
The underlined behaviors are openings in your wall. They result in guaranteed confusion—for both you and your students—more misbehavior, and slower academic progress.
This is critical because when you’re able to recognize rule-breaking when you see it—i.e. no gray areas —then being consistent in enforcing consequences becomes a lot easier.
You avoid the loopholes and frustration of seeing the same misbehavior repeated again and again.
You also avoid appearing wishy-washy and losing respect and influence.

t: One Thing You Must Ask Yourself Before Next School Year
q: If you had to pinpoint one area of classroom management in which you were weakest this past school year, what would it be?
In other words, what is your one thing , your Achilles’ heel that is mucking up all the rest?
Your one thing is undermining and making harder all your other strategies and efforts to control your classroom and enjoy teaching.
Once I started using this process with my coaching clients, we were able to zero in on the ‘why’ of their struggles almost immediately.
They also learned to their relief that they weren’t as far away from having a well-behaved class as they once thought.
Inconsistency. Moving and talking too fast. Micromanagement. Taking misbehavior personally.

t: Do You Have To Lie To Be A Good Teacher?
q: Several of her friends, who’d been listening to our conversation, chimed in with their own stories.
Because, being a straight-shooter is an easy and remarkably effective way to build trust, loyalty, and authority.
If your students believe you’re being untruthful or misleading, then they put far less stock what you say.
It’s not appropriate for me as your teacher to share that with you.

You see, when you’re the one teacher who tells it like it is , does what they say they’re going to do, and protects their freedom to form their own thoughts, ideas, and opinions, they go overboard in their appreciation for you.
Although I no longer need to teach, I have no plans of giving it up.
Students are 100% responsible for their behavior, without a doubt. However, the solutions to misbehavior, disrespect, and the like reside with the teacher.
At SCM, we do not in any circumstance advocate intimidation . No scolding. No glaring. No raising your voice.
It’s your consistent pleasantness and kindness, combined with a single-minded commitment to your classroom management plan, that gives you the leverage to manage any classroom.

Instead of charts, tokens, external rewards , bribery, manipulation, and the like, instead of trying to convince, coerce, or beg students to behave, we believe in creating a classroom they love being part of.
You have to spend some time reading and studying to ensure you really understand the SCM way and how to apply it in your classroom.
When you’re inconsistent, students believe—and rightly so—that your classroom management plan isn’t applied fairly and equally to everyone.

Respect is closely linked to likability. If your room is cluttered and you have papers strewn atop your desk, if you appear rushed and underprepared, then your students won’t view you as a leader worth following.
Not knowing what is expected for any length of time during the school day is massively frustrating for students.
They kneel down, hot-breath close and usher in learned helplessness.
Well-liked teachers are constantly assessing how their students are responding to instruction.
Lecturing, scolding, questioning, and other acts of intimidation don’t work in this day and age. They only sabotage your own peace and enjoyment and bring about more misbehavior, not less.
